## Where we stand

::: {.findings}
::: {.finding}
**This is a new model run, not a table update.** The other InVEST outputs were handed pre-computed; SWY has not been run globally yet, because a single global calibration isn't feasible. Producing an output means assembling every real input and running the model from scratch.
:::
::: {.finding}
**The orchestration is real and confirmed, not assumed.** Rich's `swy_global` + `inspring` were
read directly at the code level, not from descriptions: basin batching, per-basin routing, global-mosaic stitching, and direct CN/Kc raster overrides all work as expected. One real bug found in `inspring` itself along the way (a dead `root_depth` parameter).
:::
::: {.finding}
**The plan is test-then-scale, decided with Becky 2026-09-09: Borneo — and a complete in-house
run exists.** Quickflow (mean 406.8mm/year) and actual ET (mean 1288.0mm/year) both land in
physically plausible ranges for tropical rainforest. One genuine, diagnosable issue found, not
hidden: ~5% of local-recharge pixels show a flow-accumulation anomaly, most visibly clustered at
one coastal river-mouth location — detail below. Meeting with Becky and Rich together today,
2026-09-11.
:::
:::

## Question

> Is this project's own CN/Kc parametrization, built from
> public, peer-reviewed global products robust enough to trust at the global scale.
>
> Running end-to-end on a real study area as check (Borneo).
>
> (A stricter version of this question — does it reproduce a known, published result closely
> enough to trust scaling further — was the original framing, tested against one of Hamel et al.
> 2020's own basins. Kept as a reference in the validation section below; it isn't blocking this
> round.)

## What the model needs, and where each piece stands

| Input | Status |
|---|---|
| AOI / watershed vector | **Built** — `borneo_aoi.gpkg`, a single dissolved polygon from HydroBASINS Australia/Oceania level-6 units intersecting Borneo, built 2026-09-10 (computed area 753,803 km² vs. real ~743,330 km², 1.4% off) |
| DEM | **Sourced and verified** — SRTMGL3, 90m, via AppEEARS. Elevation range -91–4041m (Mt. Kinabalu, Borneo's real high point, is 4095m — a close, correct match) |
| Routing parameters | **Found** — Rich's `swy_global.ini` defaults (`THRESHOLD_FLOW_ACCUMULATION=1000`, `ALPHA_M=0.083333`, `BETA_I=1`, `GAMMA=1`, `MAX_PIXEL_FILL_COUNT=1000000`) |
| LULC | **Sourced and verified** — real 2020 Copernicus C3S land cover, extracted from the user's WWF OneDrive copy after this project's local file turned out to be an empty/corrupted stub (a real data-integrity finding, not a download gap). 48.1% valid fraction matches every other Borneo raster; plausible class mix (58.3% broadleaf evergreen forest) |
| Monthly precipitation | **Sourced and verified** — CHIRPS 2020, ~5.5km, clipped to Borneo. July mean 138.9mm, plausible for the region |
| Monthly ET0 | **Sourced and verified** — TerraClimate `pet` (Penman-Monteith, CO2-corrected), ~4km. Monthly means 97–118mm, plausible for tropical reference ET. **New source as of 2026-09-10** — CHIRPS is precipitation-only |
| Soil hydrologic group | **HYSOGs250m** — downloaded 2026-09-09 (global file, `data/raw/soil_hydrologic_group/`) |
| Rain events | **Placeholder used for the first run** (uniform 18 events/month) — not derived from real daily CHIRPS. The documented derivation method needs Google Earth Engine access not set up in this environment; a real gap, flagged not hidden |
| Curve number (CN) | **GCN250** as global base, confirmed sourced; biome-specific patches not yet applied for this first attempt — see below |
| Crop coefficient (Kc) | **NDVI sourced and verified** (MOD13A3, full 2000–2026 record; ~0.82 mean for a July granule, plausible for rainforest) and used directly — see below for how |
| `root_depth` | Required by the interface but confirmed dead in this model fork — satisfied with a placeholder raster, not worth sourcing carefully |

: {.terms tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

## Curve number: the harder parameter, and where the gap actually is

InVEST's own documentation is explicit that there's no global shortcut for CN — it depends on soil
group, cover type, and moisture condition, and region-specific values are preferred over blanket
defaults. **GCN250** solves the bulk of this: a purpose-built, peer-reviewed global CN product
combining land cover and soil hydrologic group. Its own authors are candid that it differentiates by
land-cover granularity, not by region-specific values *within* one land-cover class — and that the
underlying method is least validated in forested/humid environments, which is exactly this
project's LAC focus.

| Biome | Status |
|---|---|
| Tropical moist broadleaf forest | Real candidate literature found (Calero Mosquera et al. 2021, Fábrega et al. 2012) — both directly confirm the standard method overestimates runoff under tropical conditions. Patch is buildable. |
| Mangroves | No usable literature found after three separate search passes. The underlying reason: these are **tide-flooded** systems — CN's rainfall-runoff premise doesn't describe what's driving water movement here. Leaning toward documenting this as a structural limitation rather than continuing to search. |
| Flooded grasslands / savannas | Same missing-CN-number problem, but a **different mechanism**: these are **river-overflow-flooded** (seasonal inundation), not tidal. Same underlying failure mode as mangroves — a flood-pulse-dominated system CN's premise wasn't built for — just a different flood driver. The Colombian Llanos is the real, motivated test case for this specifically — sequenced after the basin validation above, not instead of it. |

: {.results}

::: {.validation-note}
**Why this matters more than it might look**: in Hamel et al. (2020)'s own sensitivity analysis,
quickflow changed by **factors of 10–13×** between antecedent-moisture CN settings in one basin. CN
is close to the dominant source of variance in this model's output, not a minor calibration knob.
:::

::: {.validation-note}
**A real architectural finding, from 2026-09-10**: `inspring`'s SWY implementation accepts CN as
a **direct raster override** (`cn_a/b/c/d_path`), not only via a lucode-indexed biophysical
table. Since GCN250 is already a per-pixel product, that's the architecturally better long-term
path — not a novel idea on our part; continuous, gridded parameterization is the norm for
physically-based hydrology models generally, and InVEST's table-based convention is a design
choice suited to its usual land-use-scenario use case. **For this first run attempt, the simpler
CSV table path was used instead** (built from GCN250's own crosswalk, no biome patches applied
yet) — lower-risk for a first pass; the raster-override path is worth a follow-up round.
:::

## Crop coefficient: a real open question, not a solved one — revised 2026-09-11

**This section's earlier framing overstated how settled this is — corrected here rather than left
standing.** The current pipeline (both Borneo and the in-progress Philippines run) computes Kc
uniformly for all vegetated classes via a linear NDVI regression (Kamble et al. 2013:
`Kc = 1.457×NDVI − 0.1725`). Rich raised a direct, well-grounded objection: **Kamble's regression
was calibrated entirely on agricultural crops** (US High Plains cropping systems), never on
forest, grassland, or any natural vegetation — applying it to forest (the majority of both AOIs'
land area) is an extrapolation outside its validated domain, not a like-for-like use. His specific
mechanism: **NDVI saturates in dense canopy** (around LAI≈3), so a linear fit built on
agricultural NDVI ranges could underestimate Kc once extrapolated to saturated forest NDVI.

Checked against two more sources rather than taken on faith:

- **Corbari et al. (2017)** measured real Kc at four eddy-covariance sites (pasture, deciduous
  forest, evergreen conifer forest — none tropical). Result: measured forest Kc came in **lower**
  than standard FAO/LAI-based assumptions, not higher — the opposite direction from Rich's
  hypothesis, though temperate-forest data doesn't settle a tropical question either way. Even
  their highest real-measured forest value is less than half what the Kamble regression predicts
  at forest-level NDVI (~0.85–0.90 → Kc≈1.07–1.14) — a sizeable discrepancy worth flagging
  regardless of which direction is ultimately right.
- **Glenn et al. (2011)** confirms the saturation mechanism directly: NDVI saturates around
  LAI≈3, EVI/SAVI don't, and EVI is established in this literature as better-correlated with
  ground-measured ET for dense canopy specifically because of this. It also cites an actual
  tropical rainforest precedent — Juarez et al. (2008), Amazonia, MODIS EVI + net radiation,
  r²=0.72–0.86 against flux towers — not yet obtained or read.

**Concrete next steps, not yet done**: switch the pipeline from NDVI to EVI (no new data source —
`_1_km_monthly_EVI` is a layer in the same MOD13A3.061 product already fetched for both Borneo and
the Philippines); read Juarez et al. (2008) for an actual tropical-forest calibration reference.
**Current forest Kc/AET numbers, Borneo included, should not be presented as validated** until
this is resolved.

Unrelated to the above, still true as originally noted: **cropland Kc** uses the same NDVI
regression rather than FAO-56 (no region-correct crop calendar built yet — Northern-Hemisphere
defaults don't fit, and oil palm/Borneo's likely dominant cropland isn't a native FAO-56 entry).
**Non-vegetated** classes (water, wetlands, bare soil, built) use fixed values from InVEST's own
guidance, unaffected by any of the above.

## The test plan

**Decided with Becky, 2026-09-09: test in Borneo.** Every raw input the model needs is downloaded
and content-verified — AOI, DEM, routing parameters, LULC, soil group, precipitation, ET0, NDVI,
and the CN base (`data/swy/borneo/inputs/`, ~1.1GB, uploaded to Drive). The CN/Kc biophysical
table and a placeholder rain-events table are built. **Two real in-house run attempts were made
2026-09-11 via Docker; the second completed cleanly.** Whole pipeline consolidated into real,
reproducible scripts: `Python_scripts/swy_borneo_run/` (see that directory's own README for the
exact pipeline and known compromises in this run). Rich has everything needed — data and scripts
both — to pick this up or extend it with his own tooling; see "Findings for Rich" below for
concrete, reproducible issues found in `inspring`'s own packaging along the way.

::: {.validation-note}
**The run outcome, plainly**: quickflow mean 406.8mm/year (range 2.3–4837.2mm), actual ET mean
1288.0mm/year — both physically reasonable for tropical rainforest, where most rainfall
infiltrates rather than running off quickly. These held identical across both run attempts.

**Two separate things worth being precise about, not conflated**:

1. **The first attempt was cut short by an infrastructure failure** — the laptop sleeping killed
   Docker's backend mid-run, which interrupted the local-recharge routing step (`L_sum`) partway
   through the basin (spatial coverage stopped almost exactly at the equator). Fixed for the
   rerun: the actual sleep cause (a battery timeout still active despite AC sleep already being
   off) plus an active keep-awake safeguard for the run's duration. **The rerun has full spatial
   coverage confirmed** (matches the stream network and quickflow rasters exactly).
2. **A separate, genuine numerical issue persists in both runs, coverage gap or not**: ~5% of
   `L_sum` pixels (4.6% in the first, incomplete run; 5.4% in the second, complete one — same
   order of magnitude) show runaway flow-accumulation values into the billions, against a median
   around 5,000. This is not an artifact of the interrupted run — it reproduced independently once
   full coverage existed to check it against. Visually, it's not random scatter either: the
   clearest cluster sits at a specific river-mouth/estuary location on the island's east coast,
   consistent with SRTM's known difficulty in flat, tidally-influenced coastal terrain (a real,
   named hypothesis, not confirmed) rather than one arbitrary DEM error. Worth investigating
   before trusting `L_sum`-derived quantities, including the aggregated baseflow figure,
   spatially — though notably, **the aggregated `qb` figure itself came out numerically identical
   between the incomplete and complete runs** (1705.005), suggesting the AOI-wide aggregate is
   more robust than the pixel-level anomaly might suggest.
:::

Two things worth being explicit about, since they're a real shift from where this research
started, not a detail:

- **The mangrove/flooded-savannas CN gap is not a blocker for her.** Resolving that patch before
  testing was this project's own caution, not a condition she set.
- **Rigorous validation against a published result isn't the priority she cares about here either**
  — testing that the pipeline actually runs on a real basin matters more right now than proving
  numerical agreement with an external benchmark.

::: {.validation-note}
**Kept for reference, not as a current requirement**: the original plan was to test against one of
Hamel et al. (2020)'s own basins (Peru or Myanmar) specifically because they have published,
granular output to check a result against — Peru's CN came from an existing calibrated SWAT model
(Uribe et al. 2013), Myanmar's from Mandle et al. (2017) (Hamel co-authored both — one small
research lineage, not independent sources). That reasoning is still scientifically sound and worth
returning to if a rigor-focused validation is wanted later; it just isn't what this round is for.
:::

## Philippines comparison — in progress, plan revised 2026-09-11

Becky couldn't locate the Borneo/Malaysia model output originally planned as a comparison target,
but shared an existing Philippines SWY run instead. Plan: replicate this project's own
from-scratch approach for the Philippines, then compare. Status:

- **AOI**: built from the Philippines workspace's own output footprint (polygonizing the valid-data
  mask of Rich's shared `QF.tif`), not independently re-derived — guarantees the same computational
  domain. A first attempt using the routing-domain files instead overshot by 46% (it includes
  ~118,000 km² of upstream-contributing Borneo terrain with zero actual retained output) — caught
  by checking the raster directly, corrected.
- **DEM, NDVI (12 months), LULC**: all landed. NASA AppEEARS' API started returning a blanket 403
  on task submission/download mid-session (unrelated to this project's requests — public metadata
  endpoints stayed open throughout); worked around via AppEEARS' own web UI, submitting a
  hand-built request JSON directly rather than through the blocked API path.
- **Not yet run**: the biophysical table and the model call itself — both scripted and ready
  (`Python_scripts/swy_philippines_run/`), waiting on the Kc question above to settle first.

**A separate, real complication**: Becky's Philippines baseline turns out not to be a single year
at all — it's a **30-year CMIP6 multi-model climatological average (1984–2014)**. This project's
own runs use real single-year 2020 data (CHIRPS, TerraClimate, MODIS). These are not directly
comparable as currently built. Options under consideration, none chosen yet: present the 2020 run
as a second, honestly-labeled data point rather than a validation; rebuild a genuine 1984–2014
climatology (NDVI/EVI could only cover 2000–2014, MODIS's actual record — a documented compromise,
not a true match); or ask Becky/Rich for their actual precip/ET0 input rasters directly.

## Findings for Rich, from actually trying to build `inspring` in Docker

Concrete and reproducible, not "it didn't work":

1. **`inspring`'s own `Dockerfile` fails immediately** on `pip3 install -r requirements.txt` —
   that file was deleted from the repo in 2022 and never replaced. Confirmed by actually running
   the build, not just reading the file.
2. **`setup.py`'s `packages` list omits `inspring.seasonal_water_yield`** — a normal `pip install
   .` compiles the Cython extension but the Python module itself isn't importable afterward.
   Worked around (not fixed upstream) via `python setup.py build_ext --inplace` + `PYTHONPATH`
   pointed at the source tree directly.
3. **Good news**: the *current* upstream `ecoshard` (not the old pinned
   `therealspring/ecoshard@b9b4580` fork commit) works fine — its bundled `ecoshard.geoprocessing`
   (with `routing`) and `ecoshard.taskgraph` have the API `inspring` expects. Resolves an earlier
   open question about whether the old fork was still required — it isn't.
4. This project's own existing Docker image
   (`therealspring/global_ncp-computational-environment`) already had everything `inspring`
   actually needs — building on top of that, rather than debugging `inspring`'s own broken
   Dockerfile, is what actually worked.

Items 1 and 2 are small, well-scoped, non-scientific fixes — real candidates for a short PR back
to `springinnovate/inspring`, not yet attempted.
